questions.prompt: Which word belongs in “Stir the ___ into the cake mixture”?
questions.explanation: Flour is the baking ingredient. The cake mixture gives you the clue.

questions.prompt: What makes flour and flower homophones?
options: They share a pronunciation but have different meanings
questions.explanation: Listen to the sound, then compare the meanings: a baking ingredient and something with petals.

questions.prompt: In “I would like a biscuit too”, what does too mean?
questions.explanation: Too can mean also. The sentence is about wanting a biscuit as well, rather than counting two.

title: Flour or flower? Homophones in everyday sentences
practice: Try Connections and look for a relationship that fits every clue. It might involve meaning, a category or another shared feature.

sections.html:
Homophones are words that sound the same but have different meanings. Turn up with flour when someone wanted a flower and you have the start of a cake, but a disappointing bouquet.

The dictionary entries for flour and flower give the same pronunciation. The sentence tells you which one belongs.
sections.title: Same sound, different meaning

sections.html:
A recipe needs flour; a vase holds a flower. The surrounding words give you the clue.

Homophone examples in sentences
SentenceMeaning
Stir the flour into the cake mixture.Baking ingredient
Put the flower in the vase.A bloom
I would like two biscuits.The number 2
I would like a biscuit too.Also

Merriam-Webster lists two, too and to as homophones.
sections.title: Flour and flower in sentences

sections.html:
Say one word for each clue. Do your answers sound alike?

  1. A baking ingredient / something with petals.
  2. A horse-shaped chess piece / the dark part of the day.
  3. The number after one / another way to say “also”.
Check the three pairs

Flour / flower. One goes in a cake; the other in a vase.

Knight / night. Merriam-Webster gives knight and night the same pronunciation.

Two / too. “I want two biscuits. You can have one too.”

Now try a silly sentence: “The knight only rides at night.”
sections.title: Try three pairs with your ears

sections.html:
Flour, sugar, butter and eggs connect through meaning: baking ingredients. Flour and flower connect through sound.

sections.title: A word puzzle can connect sounds or meanings

sections.html:
Homophones share a sound; homographs share a spelling. The terms can overlap. Merriam-Webster’s guide to word pairs explains the difference.

Accents matter: two words may sound identical to one speaker but different to another.

For a different surprise, meet words that mean their own opposite. This time the twist is in the meaning.

From sound-alikes to letter swaps, browse our short guide to English wordplay.
